abstract: Antigenic peptides are short protein sequences that are recognized by the immune system. The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) transports intracellular peptides to the cell surface, where interactions with CD8+ T cells are induced. Peptide presentation involves a complex transport pathway, which has several key checkpoints and involves kinetic proofreading. Here, we show that cell metabolism, by modulating transport checkpoints, can strongly affect antigen presentation. We predict the presentation of individual peptides from peptide-specific data - intracellular concentration and MHC binding affinity - and the transmission characteristics of the transport pathway. Together, these factors determine the total amount and the specific distribution of peptides available for T-cell recognition, depending on the metabolic state of the cell. We validate the underlying model by combining RNA-seq expression data, inferred MHC-binding constants, and mass spectrometry data for peptides presented across different cell lines. We map characteristic shifts in the presented peptidome between healthy and cancer cell lines and infer underlying changes in transport checkpoints, including variations in peptide supply and MHC expression. Together, the model establishes a predictive link between immunogenicity and the metabolic landscape of the presenting cell.
